title: Binary trees, BST, AVL, heaps and B-trees
kicker: ENCT 252 · Data Structure and Algorithms · Chapter 5
subtitle: Hierarchies that keep search fast — provided they stay balanced.

sections.title: Trees and traversals
sections.body: A tree has a root, each node has children; a node without children is a leaf; the height is the longest root-to-leaf path. A binary tree has at most two children per node. Three depth-first traversals visit the root pre, in or post the subtrees: preorder root-left-right, inorder left-root-right, postorder left-right-root. Inorder on a BST gives sorted order.

questions.prompt: Inorder traversal of a binary search tree yields…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Left subtree (smaller) first, then the node, then the larger right subtree.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — Trees and traversals
figures.note: The lab draws the pointers as a tree; inorder prints the keys sorted.

sections.title: Binary search trees
sections.body: In a BST everything in a node’s left subtree is smaller and everything in its right subtree larger. Search, insert and delete follow one root-to-leaf path: O(height). Deleting a node with two children replaces it with its inorder successor (the smallest key of the right subtree). The catch: insert sorted keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and the tree degenerates into a chain of height 5 — O(n) search.

questions.prompt: Inserting already-sorted keys into a plain BST gives…

choices.text: A chain of height n: search becomes O(n).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each new key goes to the right of the previous one.

figures.caption: Figure 5.2.1 — an unbalanced BST
figures.note: Sorted input turns the BST into a list.

sections.title: AVL trees: staying balanced
sections.body: An AVL tree keeps the heights of every node’s two subtrees within 1 (balance factor −1, 0, +1). After an insertion or deletion that breaks this, a rotation restores it: single rotations fix left-left and right-right imbalances; double rotations fix left-right and right-left. Height stays O(log n). The same keys that made a chain now give root 30 and height 3.

questions.prompt: Which rotation fixes inserting 30 under 20 under 10 (a right-right chain)?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: 20 becomes the root with 10 and 30 as children.

figures.caption: Figure 5.3.1 — AVL insertions
figures.note: Each step names the imbalance and the rotation.

problems.prompt: Insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 25 into an AVL tree. What is the final root and height?

sections.title: Heaps and priority queues
sections.body: A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array where every parent is ≤ its children (min-heap). Children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2. Insert at the end and sift up; remove the minimum by moving the last element to the root and sift down — both O(log n). Building a heap of n items is O(n). Heaps power priority queues and heap sort.

worked.why: A min-heap is stored as [2, 5, 9, 7, 6]. Where are the children of the node at index 1 (value 5)?
Children are at indexes 3 and 4: values 7 and 6, both ≥ 5, so the heap order holds there. Its parent is ⌊(1−1)/2⌋ = 0 (value 2).

questions.prompt: Where is the smallest element of a min-heap?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Every parent is ≤ its children, so the minimum cannot be below another node.

figures.caption: Figure 5.4.1 — a min-heap
figures.note: Sift up on insert, sift down on extract.

sections.title: Huffman coding
sections.body: Give frequent symbols short codes. Huffman’s algorithm repeatedly merges the two lightest trees into one, then reads the code from the path (left 0, right 1). The result is an optimal prefix code. For aaaabbc: 10 bits instead of 56. For the classic frequencies f:5 e:9 c:12 b:13 d:16 a:45 the total cost is 224 bits over 100 characters.

choices.text: No codeword is the start of another, so a bit stream decodes unambiguously.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Symbols sit at leaves of the tree.

figures.caption: Figure 5.5.1 — building the tree
figures.note: Merge the two smallest each time.

sections.title: B-trees
sections.body: A B-tree of order m has up to m−1 keys and m children per node and all leaves at the same depth. Insert into a leaf; if it overflows, split it around the median and push the median up — possibly all the way to a new root. Wide nodes make the tree shallow, so a disk search reads few blocks. Inserting 1…7 into an order-3 tree gives root key 4 and height 3.

questions.prompt: Why are B-trees used for disk indexes?

choices.text: Wide nodes keep the tree very shallow, so few disk blocks are read.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each node is sized to a disk block.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• BST operations cost O(height); AVL rotations keep height O(log n).
  • Heap = partial order in an array; Huffman = greedy merging; B-tree = wide and shallow.
